parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄρον (áron). Semantic loan from translingual Arum.
Inherited from Ancient Greek ἄτροπος (átropos, “unchangeable”). The noun sense is a semantic loan from translingual Atropa.
Calque of translingual angiosperms.
From Ancient Greek ἀδῐ́ᾰντον (adĭ́ănton). For the second sense, semantic loan from translingual Adiantum.
Borrowed from translingual Adriana.
Borrowed from translingual Aethionema, from Ancient Greek αἴθω (aíthō, “to ignite, to catch fire”) + Ancient Greek νῆμᾰ (nêmă, “thread, string”).

parole.significato: The Alismatales, an order of plants.
parole.testo: Calque of translingual Alismatales, as άλισμα (álisma, “alisma, water plantain”) + -ώδη (-ódi).

parole.significato: Any owlet moth of the genus Amphipyra.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Amphipyra.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀναγαλλίς (anagallís), with a semantic loan from translingual Anagallis.

parole.significato: any member of the genus Anacamptis of orchids
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from translingual Anacamptis. By surface analysis, ανακάμπτω (anakámpto, “to reappear, to recover, to revive”) + -ίδα (-ída, feminine suffix).
Borrowed from translingual Anthurium.

parole.significato: anthropo-, relating to man or mankind
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνθρωπo- (anthrōpo-), from ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man”). For scientific, contemporary terms Learned borrowing from translingual anthropo-.
Borrowed from translingual Anthropopithecus.
Borrowed from translingual Annona.
Borrowed from translingual Apteryx (literally “no-wing”).
Borrowed from translingual Araujia.
Calque of translingual Arachnida.
Calque of translingual Arecaceae, as αρέκα (aréka, “Areca”) + -ειδή (-eidí, “taxonomic suffix”).
Borrowed from translingual Arthropoda.
Borrowed from translingual Archaeopteryx. By surface analysis, αρχαίος (archaíos, “ancient”) + Ancient Greek πτέρῠξ (ptérŭx, “wing”).
From Ancient Greek ἀσκληπῐᾰ́ς (asklēpĭắs). Semantic loan from translingual Asclepias.
Borrowed from translingual Bacillus, from Latin bacillus.
Inherited from Koine Greek βελονίς (belonís), from Ancient Greek βελόνη (belónē). Has since developed a semantic loan from translingual Belonidae.
Borrowed from translingual Verbascum.

parole.significato: A birch, a tree of the genus Betula.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Betula, from Latin betula.

parole.significato: Any jewel beetle of the genus Buprestis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Buprestis, from Latin būprēstis, from Ancient Greek βούπρηστῐς (boúprēstĭs).
Calque of translingual Buprestidae, as βουπρήστης (vouprístis, “Buprestis”) + -ίδες (-ídes, “-idae”).

parole.significato: The Branchiopoda, the branchiopods; certain crustaceans.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Branchiopoda.
Borrowed from translingual Broussonetia.

parole.significato: The Bryophyta, the bryophytes or mosses.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Bryophyta.
From Ancient Greek βρόμος (brómos). Semantic loan from translingual Bromus.
Borrowed from translingual Gavialis.
Borrowed from translingual Garcinia.

parole.significato: The Dasyuromorphia, an order of mammals.
parole.testo: Piece-for-piece calque of translingual Dasyuromorphia, as δασύς (dasýs, “hairy”) + ουρά (ourá, “tail”) + μορφή (morfí, “shape, form”) + -α (-a, neuter plural substantive suffix).
Back-formation from δευτεροστόμια (defterostómia), from translingual Deuterostomia.
Learned borrowing from translingual Dimorphotheca. By surface analysis, δίμορφος (dímorfos, “two-shaped; two-formed”) + θήκη (thíki, “case, sheath”).
Calque of translingual Dinophyceae. By surface analysis, δίνη (díni, “vortex, whirlpool”) + φύκος (fýkos, “seaweed, alga”).

parole.significato: The Diplopoda, the diplopods or millipedes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Diplopoda.
Back-formation from διπλόποδα (diplópoda), from translingual Diplopoda.
Borrowed from translingual Ecdysozoa.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐλαίαγνος (elaíagnos), with a semantic loan from translingual Elaeagnus.
Borrowed from translingual Embiotocidae. By surface analysis, εμβιοτόκος (emviotókos, “Embiotica”) + -ίδες (-ídes).
Borrowed from translingual Entoloma.
Borrowed from translingual Hexapoda.
Borrowed from translingual Epipremnum.
Borrowed from translingual Erebidae, suffixed with -ίδες (-ídes).

parole.significato: The Ericales, an order of plants.
parole.testo: Calque of translingual Ericales, from ερείκη (ereíki, “Erica sp.”) + -ώδη (-ódi).
Borrowed from translingual Erythroxylum. By surface analysis, ερυθρός (erythrós, “red”) + ξύλο (xýlo, “wood”).
Borrowed from translingual Heteroneura.
Borrowed from translingual Eutheria.
Semantic loan from translingual Eukaryota, from ευκαρυωτικός (efkaryotikós, “eukaryotic”).
Borrowed from translingual Eumetazoa.
Borrowed from translingual Eurytides.
Borrowed from translingual Euphorbia.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐφέδρᾱ (ephédrā), with a semantic loan from translingual Ephedra.
Back-formation from εφημερόπτερα (efimeróptera), from translingual Ephemeroptera.
From translingual Echinodermata.

parole.significato: The Echinozoa, the echinozoans, certain echinoderms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Echinozoa.

parole.significato: Any seaweed or red alga of the genus Eucheuma.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Eucheuma. Equivalent to ευ- (ef-, “good”) + χεύμα (chévma, “pouring”).
Calque of translingual Theropoda.
Borrowed from translingual Thylacinus.
Borrowed from translingual Thysanoptera.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἱερᾱ́κῐον (hierā́kĭon), with a semantic loan from translingual Hieracium.

parole.significato: The Ichneumonidae, the ichneumonids or ichneumon wasps.
parole.testo: From translingual Ichneumonidae, suffixed with -ίδες (-ídes).
Borrowed from translingual Kalanchoe.
Borrowed from translingual Campanula. By surface analysis, καμπάνα (kampána, “bell”) + -ούλα (-oúla, diminutive suffix).
Borrowed from translingual Carpinus, from Latin carpinus.
Borrowed from translingual Caseasauria.
Borrowed from translingual Kentrosaurus. By surface analysis, κέντρο (kéntro) + -σαυρος (-savros).

Borrowed from Ancient Greek κεφαλόρριζον (kephalórrhizon), with a semantic loan from translingual Cephalorhizum. By surface analysis, κεφάλι (kefáli, “head”) + ρίζα (ríza, “root”) + -ο (-o, neuter suffix).
From translingual Cicadidae, suffixed with -ίδες (-ídes).
Calque of translingual Cichlidae, as Κίχλη (Kíchli, “Cichla”) + -ίδες (-ídes, “-idae”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Clematicissus.
parole.testo: Calque of translingual Clematicissus, hence the intermediate 'o' instead of 'i.' Calqued with κλήμα (klíma, “vine”) + κισσός (kissós, “ivy”).
Borrowed from translingual Coelacanthus.

parole.significato: The Coleoptera, the taxon comprised of all beetles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Coleoptera.
From the Ancient Greek κολεός (koleós). The botanical sense is a semantic loan from translingual Coleus.
Calque of translingual Corynebacterium, as κορύνη (korýni, “club”) + βακτηρίδιο (vaktirídio, “bacterium”).
Borrowed from translingual Crinoidea.
Borrowed from translingual Ctenophora. By surface analysis, Ancient Greek κτείς (kteís, “comb”) + -φόρο (-fóro, “carrier”).
Learned borrowing from translingual Cyanocorax. By surface analysis, κυανός (kyanós, “cyan”) + κόρακας (kórakas, “raven”).
From κύτταρο (kýttaro, “cell”) + μεγάλος (megálos, “large, bug”) + ιός (iós, “virus”). Calque of translingual Cytomegalovirus.

parole.significato: The Lamiales, an order of plants.
parole.testo: Calque of translingual Lamiales, as λάμιον (lámion, “Lamium”) + -ώδη (-ódi, “-ales”).
Borrowed from translingual Lantana.

parole.significato: The Lycaenidae, the lycaenids or gossamer-winged butterflies.
parole.testo: From translingual Lycaenidae, suffixed with -ίδες (-ídes). Influenced by the family’s etymological cognate, Greek λύκαινα (lýkaina, “she-wolf”).
Borrowed from translingual Lymantria.
Borrowed from translingual Magnolia.
From μαλάχη (maláchi, “mallow”) + -ώδη (-ódi), a calque of translingual Malvales.
Borrowed from translingual Mephitidae, from Mephitis, from Latin mephītis (“noxious gas”).
Borrowed from translingual Bignonia.
Back-formation from μυριάποδα (myriápoda, “Myriapoda”), from translingual Myriapoda, from Ancient Greek μῡρῐᾰ́ς (mūrĭắs, “myriad, ten thousand”) + Ancient Greek πούς (poús, “foot, leg”).
From μυρμήγκι (myrmígki, “ant”) + -ίδες (-ídes, “-idae”), a calque of translingual Formicidae.
Borrowed from translingual Nannopterum. By surface analysis, νάνος (nános, “dwarf”) + Ancient Greek πτερόν (pterón, “wing”).

parole.significato: The Nematoda, the nematodes or roundworms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νημᾰτώδης (nēmătṓdēs, “fibrous, filamentous”), with a semantic loan from translingual Nematoda.
From νήσσα (níssa, “duck”) + -ίδες (-ídes, “-idae”), a calque of translingual Anatidae.
Borrowed from translingual Nymphalidae, suffixed with -ίδες (-ídes).
Calque of translingual Nycticorax, as νύχτα (nýchta, “night”) + κόρακας (kórakas, “raven”). Contrast Ancient Greek νυκτικόραξ (nuktikórax).
Borrowed from translingual Xenopus, from Ancient Greek ξένος (xénos, “strange, foreign”) + Ancient Greek πούς (poús, “foot”).
Borrowed from translingual Oxynotus.
Learned borrowing from translingual Orthosiphon.
From Ancient Greek ὀρνιθόγαλον (ornithógalon), with a semantic loan from translingual Ornithogalum.
From Ancient Greek ὀροβάγχη (orobánkhē). Semantic loan from translingual Orobanche.

parole.significato: Any butterfly of the genus Parnassius, including the Apollo.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Parnassius, from Ancient Greek Παρνάσσῐος (Parnássĭos).
Learned borrowing from translingual Pedicularis.
Learned borrowing from translingual Platyhelminthes, as πλατύς (platýs, “wide, broad”) + έλμινθα (élmintha, “parasitic worm”) + -ας (-as, masculine nominative suffix).
From Ancient Greek πολυόμμᾰτος (poluómmătos). The noun sense is a semantic loan from translingual Polyommatus.
Borrowed from translingual Portulaca, from Latin portulāca.
Borrowed from translingual Potamochoerus. By surface analysis, ποτάμι (potámi, “river”) + χοίρος (choíros, “pig”).
Borrowed from translingual Potentilla.
Borrowed from translingual Protostomia.
Borrowed from translingual Protozoa.
From translingual Pyracantha. By surface analysis, πυρ (pyr, “fire”) + άκανθος (ákanthos, “acanthus”).
Borrowed from translingual Rhinoplax.

parole.significato: The Rosales, an order which includes many flowering plants, like the typic roses.
parole.testo: From ρόδο (ródo, “rose”) + -ώδη n pl (-ódi), a calque of translingual Rosales.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Rhytidosporum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Rhytidosporum, by surface analysis, ρυτίδα (rytída, “wrinkle”) + σπόρος (spóros, “seed”).

parole.significato: The Salticidae, the salticids or jumping spiders.
parole.testo: From translingual Salticidae, suffixed with -ίδες (-ídes).
Borrowed from translingual Sequoia.

parole.significato: Any orchid of the genus Serapias.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek σερᾱπῐᾰ́ς (serāpĭắs), with a semantic loan from translingual Serapias.

parole.significato: The Scarabaeidae, the scarabaeids or scarabs.
parole.testo: From translingual Scarabaeidae, suffixed with -ίδες (-ídes).
Borrowed from translingual Solanum.
Borrowed from translingual Suricata.

parole.significato: The Staphylinidae, the staphylinids, the rove beetles.
parole.testo: translingual Staphylinidae, suffixed with -ίδες (-ídes).
Borrowed from translingual Staphylococcus.
Calque of translingual Passeriformes, as στρούθιο (stroúthio, “sparrowling”) + -μορφα (-morfa, “-morpha”).

Back-formation from τελεόστεοι / Τελεόστεοι (teleósteoi / Teleósteoi), itself a learned borrowing from translingual Teleostei, from Ancient Greek τέλειος (téleios, “complete”) + Ancient Greek ὀστέον (ostéon, “bone”).

parole.significato: Any mite of the genus Tetranychus or related taxa.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Tetranychus. By surface analysis, τετρα- (tetra-, “four-”) + Ancient Greek ὄνῠχος (ónŭkhos, “claw”).

parole.significato: The Tettigoniidae, the tettigoniids or katydids.
parole.testo: From translingual Tettigoniidae, suffixed with -ίδες (-ídes).
Borrowed from translingual Tulipa, from Latin tulipa, from Ottoman Turkish دلبند (tülbent).
From Τρίτωνας (Trítonas, “Triton”). Likely a semantic loan from translingual Triton, an now-synonymous genus of newts (as Triturus).
Borrowed from translingual Trichoptera.

parole.significato: hyper-, super-, ultra-, trans- (often in semanic loans and calques)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑπερ- (huper-); often used as a calque of translingual hyper- or a semantic loan of French ultra-, French trans-, English super-, English over-, German über- and other similar prefixes.
Calque of translingual Balaeniceps, as φάλαινα (fálaina, “whale”) + κεφαλή (kefalí, “head”).

parole.significato: The Phasmatidae, the phasmatid stick insects.
parole.testo: From translingual Phasmatidae, suffixed with -ίδες (-ídes).

Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek φιλάδελφος (philádelphos, “sibling-loving”), with a semantic loan from translingual Philadelphus. Compare also Koine Greek φιλάδελφον (philádelphon, “philadelphus”).

parole.significato: The Squamata, the squamates, many reptiles.
parole.testo: Calque of translingual Squamata, as φολίδα (folída, “scale”) + -ωτά (-otá).
From Latin Fuchsia.
Borrowed from translingual Fritillaria.
Borrowed from translingual Choanozoa.
Borrowed from translingual Chordata.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek χρωμίς (khrōmís) (with a semantic loan from translingual Chromis), from χρῶμᾰ (khrômă, “skin, color”).
Borrowed from translingual Psychotria.
